---
title: "Lookup Tables"
editor: visual
---

Suppose that you want to perform an operation $f(a,b)$. Recall that $a,b \in \{0,...,n-1\}$ and that $a,b$ are stored as roots of unity $\zeta^a, \zeta^b$ where $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/n}$. The desired output may be a value in either root of unity form or as a regular encoded value.

Since there are finitely many possible inputs, we could calculate every possible value of $f(a,b)$ beforehand, without encryption. Then, when we receive encrypted inputs, we would like to use this table to obtain the encrypted answer.

This is the idea behind lookup tables. In our applications, they are relevant to modular multiplication, inverses when they exist, sign functions, and more.

One approach is to interpolate a polynomial that gives the desired output at every possible input. Evaluating this polynomial on the encrypted inputs then performs the lookup. The table and polynomial coefficients can be public while the inputs and resulting output remain encrypted.

Chung, Kim, Kim, and Lee [@chung2024] use this approach with inputs encoded as roots of unity. Suppose there are $n$ possible values. For a lookup table $T$ with one input, we construct a polynomial satisfying $$
f(\zeta^a)=\zeta^{T(a)}.
$$ There are $n$ interpolation points, so the polynomial has at most degree $n-1$.

For operations with multiple inputs, we will consider two approaches. First, we will consider the approach which interpolates a polynomial in multiple variables while keeping inputs separate. Then, we will consider the approach which combines inputs into a single value and interpolates a single variable polynomial.

### Multivariable Interpolation

Chung, Kim, Kim, and Lee [@chung2024] use multivariable interpolation. For example, modular multiplication requires a polynomial satisfying $$
f(\zeta^a,\zeta^b)=\zeta^{ab}.
$$

Instead of combining two inputs into a single value, Chung, Kim, Kim, and Lee construct a polynomial in two variables. Suppose each input is an $n$-th root of unity. Let $d_{ab}$ be the desired encoded output for the input pair $(\zeta^a,\zeta^b)$. We want a polynomial satisfying $$
f(\zeta^a,\zeta^b)=d_{ab}
$$ for every possible pair of inputs.

### Example: $n=4$

Each input is a fourth root of unity.

The lookup table has sixteen entries: $$
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 & v=1 & v=\zeta & v=\zeta^2 & v=\zeta^3\\
\hline
u=1       & d_{00} & d_{01} & d_{02} & d_{03}\\
u=\zeta   & d_{10} & d_{11} & d_{12} & d_{13}\\
u=\zeta^2 & d_{20} & d_{21} & d_{22} & d_{23}\\
u=\zeta^3 & d_{30} & d_{31} & d_{32} & d_{33}
\end{array}
$$

First, hold the second input fixed at $v=\zeta^b$. We can interpolate a polynomial $p_b(u)$ satisfying $$
p_b(\zeta^a)=d_{ab},
\qquad a=0,1,2,3.
$$

Each $p_b$ has degree at most three. Doing this for every column gives four polynomials. $$
p_0(u),\quad p_1(u),\quad p_2(u),\quad p_3(u).
$$

Next, we need to select the correct column using $v$. Define the Lagrange polynomials $$
L_b(v)=
\prod_{\substack{0\leq k\leq 3\\k\neq b}}
\frac{v-\zeta^k}{\zeta^b-\zeta^k}.
$$

These satisfy

$$
L_b(\zeta^k)=
\begin{cases}
1,&k=b,\\
0,&k\neq b.
\end{cases}
$$ For example, $$
L_0(v)=
\frac{(v-\zeta)(v-\zeta^2)(v-\zeta^3)}
{(1-\zeta)(1-\zeta^2)(1-\zeta^3)}.
$$

We can now combine the column polynomials: $$
f(u,v)=
p_0(u)L_0(v)+p_1(u)L_1(v)
+p_2(u)L_2(v)+p_3(u)L_3(v).
$$ When $v=\zeta^b$, all terms go to 0 except $p_b(u)$. Thus, $$
f(\zeta^a,\zeta^b)=p_b(\zeta^a)=d_{ab},
$$ as desired.

The column polynomials themselves can be written as $$
p_b(u)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}d_{ab}L_a(u).
$$ Substituting gives

$$
\boxed{
f(u,v)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\sum_{b=0}^{3}
d_{ab}L_a(u)L_b(v).
}
$$

Each Lagrange polynomial has degree three, so $f$ has degree at most three in each variable. After expanding, it has the form $$
f(u,v)=\sum_{i=0}^{3}\sum_{j=0}^{3}A_{ij}u^iv^j.
$$ There are sixteen coefficients, but the total degree is at most six, coming from the term $u^3v^3$.

### Combining Inputs

Alternatively, we could encode a pair of elements as a single value, and then interpolate a polynomial in one variable. We can do all of this publicly beforehand, so only evaluating the polynomial needs to happen in an encrypted setting.

We might consider something like

$$
t(w,z)=nw+z.
$$

This distinguishes every ordered pair of $n$th roots of unity, and gives $n^2$ points to interpolate on. Thus, the lookup table may be represented as polynomial of degree at most $n^2-1$. Although the polynomial is higher degree, this method has a particular advantage with symmetric functions.

### Exploiting Symmetry

Consider the case of modular multiplication. This operation is symmetric. That is, $f(a,b) = f(b,a)$. It seems reasonable that with symmetry, we should be able to simplify our lookup table in some way.

::: {#fig-symmetric-lookup}
$$
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 & b=0 & b=1 & b=2 & b=3\\
\hline
a=0
& d_{00}
& \textcolor[RGB]{230,159,0}{d_{01}}
& \textcolor[RGB]{86,180,233}{d_{02}}
& \textcolor[RGB]{0,158,115}{d_{03}}\\
a=1
& \textcolor[RGB]{230,159,0}{d_{10}}
& d_{11}
& \textcolor[RGB]{204,121,167}{d_{12}}
& \textcolor[RGB]{213,94,0}{d_{13}}\\
a=2
& \textcolor[RGB]{86,180,233}{d_{20}}
& \textcolor[RGB]{204,121,167}{d_{21}}
& d_{22}
& \textcolor[RGB]{0,114,178}{d_{23}}\\
a=3
& \textcolor[RGB]{0,158,115}{d_{30}}
& \textcolor[RGB]{213,94,0}{d_{31}}
& \textcolor[RGB]{0,114,178}{d_{32}}
& d_{33}
\end{array}
$$

A symmetric lookup table for $n=4$.
:::

The current construction does not use the symmetry of the table, because $t(w,z)\neq t(z,w)$ when $w\neq z$. Ideally, they would be equal so that we can use fewer interpolation points and get a lower degree.

So, we want to create a function $t(w,z)$ such that $t(w,z)=t(u,v)$ if and only if

$$
(u,v)=(w,z)\quad\text{or}\quad(u,v)=(z,w).
$$

Instead, consider something with a nonlinear term:

$$
t(w,z)=w+z+c wz.
$$

This is symmetric, but we need to choose $c$ so that two different unordered pairs do not give the same value.

If two pairs give the same value, then

$$
w+z+c wz=u+v+c uv,
$$

so

$$
c(wz-uv)=u+v-w-z.
$$

If $wz=uv$, then their sums must also be equal. Having the same sum and product means they are the same unordered pair.

Otherwise, there is just one value of $c$ that would make these two pairs collide:

$$
c=\frac{u+v-w-z}{wz-uv}.
$$

Since there are only finitely many pairs, there are only finitely many values of $c$ to avoid. So we can choose a $c$ that works.

Then, we interpolate a polynomial $q$ such that

$$
q\bigl(t(\zeta^a,\zeta^b)\bigr)=\zeta^{ab}.
$$

Now we only need one interpolation point for each unordered pair. This gives us $n(n+1)/2$ points instead of $n^2$, and therefore a degree bound of $n(n+1)/2-1$ instead of $n^2-1$.

For example, let $n=3$ and let $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Then

$$
\zeta^3=1
$$

In this case, we can choose $c=1$, giving

$$
t(w,z)=w+z+wz.
$$

We only need to consider the following six unordered pairs:

$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(w,z) & t(w,z) & \text{Desired output } \zeta^{ab} \\
\hline
(1,1)         & 3          & 1 \\
(1,\xi)       & 1+2\zeta     & 1 \\
(1,\xi^2)     & 1+2\zeta^2   & 1 \\
(\xi,\xi)     & 2\zeta+\zeta^2      & \zeta \\
(\xi,\xi^2)   & \zeta^2 +\zeta + 1          & \zeta^2 \\
(\xi^2,\xi^2) & 2\zeta^2+\zeta    & \zeta\\
(\xi^2,1)     & 1+2\zeta^2   & 1 \\
(\xi^2,\xi)   & \zeta^2+\zeta+1  & \zeta^2 \\
(\xi^2,\xi^2)     & 2\zeta^2 + \zeta   & \zeta \\
\end{array}
$$

There are six values in the middle column which are distinct, so we can interpolate a polynomial $q$ of degree at most $5$ with these inputs and outputs. We also notice that values which aren't distinct have corresponding flipped $w$ and $z$ values.

Explicitly, label the interpolation points

$$
(t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3,t_4,t_5)
=
(3,1+2\zeta,1+2\zeta^2,\zeta-1,0,\zeta^2-1).
$$

Let

$$
L_j(T)=
\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le 5\\k\ne j}}
\frac{T-t_k}{t_j-t_k}.
$$

Then our polynomial is

$$
q(T)=L_0(T)+L_1(T)+L_2(T)
+\zeta L_3(T)+\zeta^2L_4(T)+\zeta L_5(T).
$$

Thus, for any $a,b\in\{0,1,2\}$,

$$
q\left(\zeta^a+\zeta^b+\zeta^{a+b}\right)=\zeta^{ab}.
$$

We can construct $q$ publicly beforehand. Given encrypted inputs $w$ and $z$, we would then evaluate $q(w+z+wz)$.

### Exploiting Symmetry with Multivariate Interpolation

We can also use symmetry to our advantage while keeping variables separate. Since our polynomial represents a symmetric function, $(P(u,v)=P(v,u))$. In the expanded form, $$
P(u,v)=\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}A_{ij}u^iv^j,
$$ we therefore have $(A_{ij}=A_{ji})$. This lets us group terms with matching coefficients as follows. $$
P(u,v)
=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{ii}(uv)^i
+\sum_{0\le i<j\le n-1}
A_{ij}(uv)^i\left(u^{j-i}+v^{j-i}\right).
$$ We can compute the powers of $(uv)$ and the sums $(u^k+v^k)$ instead of individually multiplying every term $u^iv^j$

To compute the $(u^k+v^k)$, we can use factorization. For example, since $i^2=-1$, $$
u^2+v^2=(u+iv)(u-iv).
$$ This requires only one multiplication, rather than the two needed to square $u$ and $v$ separately.

We would like to generalize this for $k > 2$. We know that we can factor any polynomial using its complex roots.

First, consider the single variate case: $$
x^k+1=\prod_{i=1}^k(x-r_i).
$$ Where $r_i$ is the $i$-th $k$-th root of $-1$ .

When $v = 0$ our problem is trivial. For $v\neq 0$, substitute $x=u/v$ to get $$
\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^k+1
=\prod_{i=1}^k\left(\frac{u}{v}-r_i\right).
$$

Multiplying by $v^k$ and distributing gives $$
u^k+v^k=\prod_{r=1}^k(u-r_iv).
$$

Evaluating this requires $k-1$ multiplications. This can be more efficient for small $k$, but is not efficient for larger $k$.

### Example: Construction and Contrasting of Modular Multiplication for n = 4

Below are the two methods of polynomial interpolation on the multiplication table with $n = 4$.

Bivariate interpolation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(u,v)=\frac14\bigl[&
1+v+v^2+v^3\\
&+u(1-iv-v^2+iv^3)\\
&+u^2(1-v+v^2-v^3)\\
&+u^3(1+iv-v^2-iv^3)
\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

For the bivariate method, calculating $u^2,u^3,v^2,v^3$ takes four multiplications. There are also nine mixed terms $u^iv^j$ with $i,j\in\{1,2,3\}$, giving thirteen multiplications altogether.

This method needs only three layers: two to obtain powers through $u^3$ and $v^3$, and one more for the mixed terms.


With symmetry grouping, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(u,v)=\frac14\bigl[
&1+(u+v)+(u^2+v^2)+(u^3+v^3)-iuv\\
&-uv(u+v)+iuv(u^2+v^2)+(uv)^2\\
&-(uv)^2(u+v)-i(uv)^3
\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$

We can evaluate this in three multiplication layers:
$$
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
\text{Layer} & \text{Values computed} & \text{Multiplications}\\
\hline
1 & u^2,\ v^2,\ uv & 3\\
2 & u^3=u^2u,\ v^3=v^2v,\ (uv)^2,\ 
    uv(u+v),\ uv(u^2+v^2) & 5\\
3 & (uv)^2(u+v),\ (uv)^3=(uv)^2(uv) & 2
\end{array}
$$
Thus, this evaluation uses $3+5+2=10$ multiplications and has multiplicative depth $3$.




For the single-variable polynomial, let $c=2$.  Thus, 

$$
t(u,v)=u+v+2uv.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q(t)=1+\frac{1}{7072000}\bigl[&
(12507520-191360i)t\\
&+(3844256-421408i)t^2\\
&-(2688960+341120i)t^3\\
&-(1056912+124384i)t^4\\
&-(173756+8892i)t^5\\
&-(47656+2392i)t^6\\
&-(24280+1560i)t^7\\
&+(4092+1144i)t^8\\
&+(3181+117i)t^9
\bigr].
\end{aligned}
$$
For the combined-input method, calculating $t=u+v+cuv$ takes one multiplication. Then, calculating $t^2,\ldots,t^9$ takes eight more. This method has multiplicative depth 5: One layer to calculate $t$, and four more to get all powers through $t^9$.


Overall, the bivariate method has lower multiplicative depth but a greater number of multiplications. 

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
& \text{Univariate}
& \text{Bivariate}
& \text{Bivariate with symmetry}\\
\hline
\text{Encrypted multiplications} & 9 & 13 & 10\\
\text{Multiplicative depth} & 5 & 3 & 3
\end{array}
$$
